extracted.intended_audience: British statesmen, educated public, and political thinkers concerned with the French Revolution (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reasoning for a conservative political essay reflecting on the French Revolution: diagnosing causes of public disorder, defending institutions, and recommending reform over abolition. Targets readers persuadable by historical, moral, and practical argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of the nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not presume the nobility were generally corrupt or principal oppressors; evaluate their actual conduct (honor, hospitality, military tone, humane behavior toward inferior classes) rather than accept party denunciations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites direct observation: nobles often well-bred, humane, frank in conversation, fair as landlords, and not the administrators of the most grievous parts of government. Exceptions may exist but should be treated as such; reforms short of abolition are recommended. Avoid blanket degradation ('to degrade is to punish').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish vices from pretexts (causes vs pretexts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the true causes of public disorder (pride, ambition, avarice, revenge, lust, sedition, hypocrisy, ungoverned zeal) rather than attacking the names, titles, or institutions that serve as pretexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History should be used to teach causes of error; remedies must target the permanent causes (vices), not transitory organs or names. Changing names or removing a class of officers will not cure the underlying vice and may renew the mischief in new forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of history
rubrics_metrics.description: Use history to draw instructive moral and causal lessons, not as a magazine of weapons for party vengeance or to pervert the past to justify present persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware perversion of history to supply 'offensive and defensive weapons' for parties; do not gibbeting the carcass of past abuses while current practical evils continue. Historical examples should obscure petty party colors and illuminate moral quality of actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against collective punishment of corporate bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not punish entire corporate bodies (clergy, nobility, nations) for the crimes of some predecessors or members; corporate immortality protects members' good, not their collective punishment for ancestral offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unjust to chastise men for offences of their natural ancestors; the Assembly's wholesale punishment of clergy and nobles is condemned. Corporate punishments foster injustice and revenge rather than reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of property and prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect established property rights and the doctrine of prescription as elements of natural law; legislative bodies should not arbitrarily confiscate or disrupt settled property relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscations of church lands and other possessions (and treating speculative paper as lawful tender) are criticized as destroying property and stability. Shaking prescription imperils all property when power tempts seizure; legislation should secure, not destroy, property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reform to abolition of institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor measured reform within existing institutions over their wholesale abolition; many abuses can be corrected without destroying the institution itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noblesse and clergy had faults but not 'incorrigible vices'; short reforms could remove abuses. Abolition risks producing worse outcomes (loss of learning, erosion of character, social ruin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against theatrical or literary incitement to vengeance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use plays, spectacles, or publications that dramatize past crimes merely to inflame public hatred or to prepare the populace for persecution of current groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: staging the St. Bartholomew massacre to excite loathing of the clergy — such spectacles teach hatred rather than temper public virtue. Cultural productions can stimulate 'cannibal appetites' and alertness to new murders.

rubrics_metrics.name: True toleration vs contempt disguised as toleration
rubrics_metrics.description: Toleration is genuine when it arises from respect for the value of religious opinions and for justice; mere indifference or contempt for opinions is not true toleration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English model praised: men who favor and protect religions because they respect a common principle. Critique of those who 'tolerate' because they think opinions unimportant — equal neglect is not impartial kindness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lowering clerical quality via election and pillage
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not replace a regulated clerical establishment with elective, politicized appointments and plunder of revenues, since that will drive out sober, learned clergy and invite electioneering intrigues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective clergy and degraded pensions will attract licentious, crafty, factious men and expel men of science and independence; the Assembly's confiscations and elective provisions are likely to ruin clerical character and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert legal claim into vexatious extortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish lawful clerical claims from oppressive or vexatious exactions; reforms should correct extortion without presuming every legal claim is unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author interrogates whether clergy 'used to exceed due demands' or 'convert a legal claim into a vexatious extortion' — suggesting such questions deserve careful, evidence-based inquiry rather than wholesale condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address social causes of aristocratic decline (permeability of ranks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that strict separation between aristocracy and wealthy commons (exclusion of wealthy commoners from rank/military) contributes to social resentment and the decline of the old nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive punctilio between orders and reserving military rank to men of family are cited as causes; a permanent assembly sharing power would have abolished invidious distinctions and corrected faults by widening occupations and pursuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware philosophical fanaticism replacing religion with civic schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be skeptical of schemes that propose replacing religion with a philosophically-founded 'civic education' that claims to retrain self-interest into public interest — such plans risk destroying religion and substituting uncertain social engineering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques the design of 'Civic Education' to supply what religion provides; warns that enthusiasts avow a state's ability to subsist without religion and predict this will culminate in abolition of Christianity once ministers are brought into contempt.
